```{=html}
<ol>
<li>The records sit furthest below the maker's curve at 11–12 m/s, 239 kW on average: gusts smooth the curve's corner at rated speed.</li>
<li>With fixed settings, the 90% band is widest where there are no records; records up to 15.5 m/s cut its mean width from 1,220 kW (16 records) to 576 kW (32).</li>
<li>The 16 records choose a length-scale of 4.6 m/s, noise 80 kW and signal size 780 kW (maximum likelihood on a grid of 3,808 settings).</li>
<li>RMSE on its own records against 400 new ones: 75 kW and 126 kW for the records' choice; 2 kW and 506 kW for a very short length-scale.</li>
<li>On 400 new records the 90% band holds 95.5% (sampling alone: about ± 3 points): 99% at 3–8 m/s, 88% at 8–13 m/s, 100% at 13–20 m/s.</li>
<li>Adding the maker's curve as a second source cuts the RMSE from 126 kW to 85 kW and the band's mean width from 391 kW to 287 kW; the band holds 92.0% overall but 82% at 8–13 m/s (one source: 88%).</li>
<li>Two sources are 41 kW closer with 16 records and 5 kW with 64.</li>
<li>With a load-reducing mode above 12.5 m/s that the maker's curve leaves out, the two-source band holds 58% of new records at 13–20 m/s; the one-source band holds 100%.</li>
<li>In that case pinball loss rates the two fits about equal (27.9 and 27.7 kW), while RMSE is 92 kW and 107 kW.</li>
</ol>

<li><b>Fits:</b> a squared-exponential kernel and one noise level; settings by maximum likelihood on a fixed grid. Settings for 24 to 64 records are stored with the page and checked by its test.</li>
```

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m9-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Surrogate</dt><dd>A cheap stand-in for something costly to run or to measure, fitted to a few samples.</dd>
<dt>Gaussian process</dt><dd>A smooth best guess with a band: narrow near the records, wide where there are none.</dd>
<dt>Length-scale and noise</dt><dd>How far one record reaches, and how much scatter the fit expects around the curve.</dd>
<dt>Held-out records</dt><dd>Records the fit never saw; only they show how good it is.</dd>
<dt>Calibration</dt><dd>A 90% band should hold about 90% of new records, overall and within each range of wind speed.</dd>
<dt>Two sources</dt><dd>A cheap curve that covers every speed, plus a few costly records; it helps when its shape is right.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The formulas: the fit, its band and the records' choice</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Symbols.** $v$ wind speed (m/s); $y$ the records' power, one entry per record (kW); $n$ the number of records; $I$ the $n \times n$ identity matrix; $^\top$ the transpose, rows written as columns ([K6](k06-vectors-matrices.html)); $|K|$ the determinant of $K$; $\sigma$ the band's standard deviation.
- **Kernel.** $k(v, v') = s_f^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{(v - v')^2}{2\ell^2}\right)$, with $\ell$ the length-scale (m/s) and $s_f$ the signal size (kW); the records carry noise $s_n$ (kW): $K = [k(v_i, v_j)] + s_n^2 I$.
- **Mean.** A basis $h(v)$ sets the shape far from the records: $[1]$ for one source, $[1,\ f(v)/1000]$ with the maker's curve $f$ for two. $H$ stacks $h$ at every record, one row each. Its weights come from generalized least squares, $\hat\beta = (H^\top K^{-1} H)^{-1} H^\top K^{-1} y$.
- **Prediction.** $m(v) = h(v)^\top \hat\beta + k_v^\top K^{-1}(y - H\hat\beta)$, where $k_v$ lists $k(v, v_i)$ for every record.
- **Band.** The curve's variance is $s_f^2 - k_v^\top K^{-1} k_v + u^\top (H^\top K^{-1} H)^{-1} u$ with $u = h(v) - H^\top K^{-1} k_v$; a new record adds $s_n^2$. The 90% band is $m \pm 1.645\,\sigma$.
- **Solving.** One Cholesky factor $K = LL^\top$ gives every solve; it costs about $n^3/3$ operations, which is why GP training sets stay small (vectors and matrices: [K6](k06-vectors-matrices.html)).
- **The records' choice.** Maximize $\log p(y) = -\tfrac12 r^\top K^{-1} r - \tfrac12 \log|K| - \tfrac n2 \log 2\pi$, $r = y - H\hat\beta$, over a grid of $\ell \times s_f \times s_n$; the page's grid has 3,808 settings.
- **Pinball loss.** For quantile level $\tau$ and forecast quantile $q$: $\tau (y - q)$ if $y \ge q$, else $(1-\tau)(q - y)$; the page averages it over the 19 levels 5% to 95% of $N(m, \sigma^2)$.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Two sources in the literature, and surrogates of slow models</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Kennedy and O'Hagan's form.** The costly source is $\rho$ times the cheap one plus an independent GP for the gap. Here the cheap curve is known exactly at every speed, so it enters as a basis function; when the cheap source is itself a slow model, both levels get a GP.
- **Nonlinear fusion.** When the costly source is not a scaled copy of the cheap one, nonlinear multi-fidelity models put the cheap output in as an extra input; the lab's open code compares both.
- **Slow models.** The same fit replaces a model too slow to run a thousand times: run it at a few inputs, fit the GP, then sample the GP, as [M7](m07-monte-carlo.html) did with its fast toy. The lab's practice task 4 does this for M7's model.
- **Scores across sites.** When a fit must work at places with no records, hold out whole places, not single records: [M10](m10-ml-forecasting.html) splits by time for the same reason.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself, then try it
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m9-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="guarantee" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A Gaussian process's 90% band holds 90% of new records at every wind speed.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In step 5 it held 99% at 3–8 m/s but 88% at 8–13 m/s. A band is only as good as its kernel and noise assumptions: check it on held-out records, by range.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cheap" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Adding a cheap second source can only make a fit better.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. With the load-reducing mode, the two-source band held 58% of new records at 13–20 m/s against the one-source band's 100%: cheap data mislead where they are wrong and no record corrects them.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="own" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A fit that passes close to all its records is a good fit.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The very short length-scale in step 4 missed its own records by 2 kW and new ones by 506 kW.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m9">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="chance" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 90% band holds 86% of 400 new records. Two standard errors of a share near 90% are √(0.9 × 0.1 ÷ 400) × 2 = 3 points. What do you conclude?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Nothing: 86% is close to 90%</li><li data-value="b">The band is likely too narrow: 4 points below is outside the sampling range</li><li data-value="c">The band is too wide</li><li data-value="d">The records are wrong</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Likely too narrow: 86% is 4 points below 90%, outside the approximate 95% sampling range of ± 3 points for independent records, so sampling alone is unlikely to explain it. Consecutive real records are not independent, so their range is wider.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="gap" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">You fit a one-source GP to 16 records, all below 12 m/s. Where will its band be widest?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">At 6 m/s, where records are dense</li><li data-value="b">At rated speed, where the curve bends</li><li data-value="c">Above 12 m/s, beyond the last record</li><li data-value="d">The same everywhere</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Above 12 m/s: with no records there, the fit falls back on its mean and its band opens up.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-case-try">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Try it yourself with open code</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Optional, about 30 minutes each; needs Python 3.10 or later (<a href="b02-python-data.html">lesson B2</a>).</p>
<p><b>Try it yourself:</b> the framework fits the three models to an invented turbine type and wind farm in a few seconds. Change the training size and the kernel-density bandwidth, or compare linear and nonlinear fusion on a test function. Its numbers say nothing about any real turbine.</p>
<ul>
<li>Clone and install it (its README's quick start), then run <code>python examples/sensitivity.py</code>: compare the three models' RMSE at 50, 100, 200 and 400 training points.</li>
<li>Run <code>python examples/probabilistic.py</code> and read the coverage at each nominal level, as in step 5.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/mfgpr-wind-power-curve">mfgpr-wind-power-curve</a>: public example repository · MIT licence · synthetic data.</p>
<p><b>Try it yourself:</b> the framework runs end to end on invented plants in about half a minute; another example compares target choices against a negative control. Its numbers say nothing about any real plant, data product or forecast system.</p>
<ul>
<li>Run <code>python examples/minimal.py</code>: in its printed scores, does each model beat the constant baseline?</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/wind-uq-surrogate">wind-uq-surrogate</a>: public example repository · MIT licence · synthetic data.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">This work was developed based upon funding from the Alliance for Sustainable Energy, LLC, Managing and Operating Contractor for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory for the U.S. Department of Energy.</p>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Where this came up in research</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:uq-mfgpr"><p>From the course author's research: a wind turbine's real power curve is a band, not a line. Adding the turbine's theoretical curve to about two hundred measurements can narrow that band, but whether it helps depends on how the fit is scored. (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1115/detc2023-114762">Li et al., ASME IDETC 2023</a>)</p></blockquote>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:uq-mfgpr"><p>Linear (autoregressive) and nonlinear multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression fuse the turbine type's theoretical power curve (low fidelity) with a few hundred kernel-density-sampled <span class="lx-term" data-term="scada">SCADA</span> points from the open <span class="lx-term" data-term="sdwpf">SDWPF</span> dataset (high fidelity), and are compared with single-fidelity regression on point and probabilistic metrics.</p><p>The kernel density sample keeps the shape of the scatter without manual cleaning; a compact training set matters because a Gaussian process solve grows with the cube of the training points.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1115/detc2023-114762">Li et al., ASME IDETC 2023</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:wind-uq"><p>In a research project (2022–2023), the course author worked on this question: can uncertainty metrics of a wind power model's inputs (weather data products, forecast ensembles and turbine-level data) predict calibrated plant-level power uncertainty at wind plants that have no power measurements?</p><p>The course author developed the surrogate-modeling workflow: calibrated uncertainty targets, surrogate models and validation on held-out plants.</p><p>Inputs: uncertainty metrics of four kinds: how a series varies over time (moving windows), how data sources disagree, how widely a forecast ensemble spreads, and how values vary across a plant's turbines (a variogram).</p><p>Targets: at plants with power measurements, the scale of a predictive distribution around the point forecast, chosen to minimize pinball loss.</p><p>Surrogates: Gaussian process regression and other regressors learn a mapping from the metrics to that scale, then predict probabilistic power at plants without measurements.</p><p>Validation holds out whole plants, scored with <span class="lx-term" data-term="pinball-loss">pinball loss</span>, <span class="lx-term" data-term="crps">CRPS</span> and <span class="lx-term" data-term="calibration">reliability</span>, with recalibration of the predictive distributions.</p><p>A surrogate is useful only if it beats a constant baseline on held-out plants.</p><p>The project has no paper. The public framework is a fresh implementation tested on synthetic data; project data and results are not public.</p><footer>This work was developed based upon funding from the Alliance for Sustainable Energy, LLC, Managing and Operating Contractor for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory for the U.S. Department of Energy.</footer></blockquote>
<p>This page's turbine is a toy: invented round numbers, not the studies' data, equations or results.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>

<li>Kennedy, M. C., and O'Hagan, A. (2000). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/87.1.1">Predicting the output from a complex computer code when fast approximations are available</a>. <em>Biometrika</em>, 87(1), 1–13. Two sources.</li>
<li>Gneiting, T., and Raftery, A. E. (2007). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1198/016214506000001437">Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation</a>. <em>Journal of the American Statistical Association</em>, 102(477), 359–378. Pinball loss and calibration.</li>
<li>Li et al. (2023). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1115/detc2023-114762">A Multi-Fidelity Gaussian Process Regression Method for Probabilistic Wind Farm Power Curve Estimation</a>. Proceedings of the ASME 2023 IDETC-CIE, Volume 3A: 49th Design Automation Conference, V03AT03A034.</li>
```
